Eliminate $z$: (1)+(3) gives $2x+3y=8$; (2)−(1) gives $x-2y=-3$ **(M1)(A1)**

Solve: $x=2y-3\Rightarrow 7y=14$, so $y=2$, $x=1$, $z=3$ **(A2)**

prompt:
Consider the system
$$\begin{aligned}x+2y-z&=1\\2x+3y+z&=4\\3x+5y+kz&=m\end{aligned}$$

**(a)** Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. **[2]**

**(b)** For this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. **[2]**

**(c)** For these values of $k$ and $m$, find the general solution. **[3]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Adding the first two equations gives $3x+5y+0z=5$ **(M1)**. The third equation's left side is a combination of the first two exactly when $k=0$ **(A1)** (equivalently, the determinant of the coefficients is zero).

**(b)** Then the third equation must be $3x+5y=5$ to be consistent, so $m=5$ **(A1)**; if $m\ne5$ the planes have no common point **(R1)**.

**(c)** Let $z=t$: $x+2y=1+t$ and $2x+3y=4-t$ **(M1)**

$y=3t-2$, $x=5-5t$ **(A1)**; general solution $(x,y,z)=(5-5t,\ 3t-2,\ t)$, $t\in\mathbb{R}$ — a line of intersection **(A1)**
